stances.claim: The 27-year delay between filing (1991-1995) and conviction (2018) is attributable to systemic factors -- inhibitions of former ponentes, midstream amendments, multiple motions to quash reaching the SC, Ombudsman reinvestigations, prosecution and defense postponements -- not to the current ponente, Justice Mañalac, who was appointed only December 8, 2017 and diligently produced a 70-page single-spaced decision with 226 footnotes in under a year.

Imelda could not be charged with plunder because the Anti-Plunder Law was enacted AFTER Marcos was ousted -- making the only available charge under the 1973 Constitution the Anti-Graft Law (RA 3019), which is bailable and produces less severe consequences than plunder would have.

Forfeiture of ill-gotten wealth was not part of the criminal judgment because separate civil suits were instituted to recover the Swiss-foundation millions -- the criminal judgment did, however, perpetually disqualify Imelda from holding any public office.

Imelda's same-day release on Nov 16, 2018 is procedurally strange in three ways: only PJ Lagos signed the release order (not the two division members Mendoza-Arcega and Mañalac); her 'Motion for Leave of Court to Avail of Post-Conviction Remedies' had not yet been ruled upon; and the prosecution did not object -- meekly accepting the bail grant.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-strange-fact enumeration (procedural anomalies as analytical concern)

notable_anecdotes: The six-question opening cascade -- 'Why did it take all of 27 years? Why was she not jailed after being convicted? Why was she granted bail? Why was her ill-gotten wealth not forfeited? Why was she convicted only of graft? Why not of plunder?' -- capturing the public's befuddlement in a single salvo before CJ provides systematic answers.
Justice Mañalac's gargantuan task: 'she had to peruse minutely the gargantuan 5-foot-thick court records' -- physicalizing the literal volume of paperwork a new SBN appointee inherited and processed.

The named-witness list -- former PM Cesar Virata, former CB Governor Jaime Laya, former SG Frank Chavez, former Ambassador Luis Ascalon -- quietly establishing that the conviction rests on testimony from credentialed government insiders.

The 226-footnote-buttressed 70-page decision with unassailable logic patiently traversing each element of 10 offenses -- making Mañalac's diligence the column's defensive shield against critics who might attribute the delay (or any acquittals) to inadequate work.

Triple strangeness: only PJ Lagos signing the release order, the 'Motion for Leave' not yet ruled upon, and the prosecution's meek non-objection -- flagged as the column's most consequential procedural-anomaly inventory.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban systematically answers the six questions befuddling readers about Imelda Marcos's conviction: why it took 27 years, why she was not jailed, why she was granted bail, why her ill-gotten wealth was not forfeited, why she was convicted only of graft, and why not of plunder. He explains that of the 10 cases lodged against her, five were filed by the Office of the Ombudsman on December 16, 1991, one on December 21, 1993, and four on August 17, 1995 -- alleging the use of Swiss foundations by Imelda and Ferdinand Marcos to hide wealth -- and were raffled to different Sandiganbayan divisions before consolidation in the Fifth Division. The delay was attributable to inhibitions of former ponentes, midstream amendments of charges, multiple motions to quash that had to reach and be decided by the Supreme Court, Ombudsman reinvestigations, and numerous postponements by both sides; the prosecution and defense memoranda were submitted only on August 29 and September 19, 2017. The new ponente, Justice Maryann E. Corpus-Mañalac -- appointed to the Sandiganbayan only on December 8, 2017 -- cannot be blamed for the delay; she diligently perused the gargantuan five-foot-thick records and produced a 70-page, single-spaced decision buttressed by 226 footnotes, convicting Imelda in seven of ten offenses and acquitting her in three. Imelda was convicted under the Anti-Graft Law (RA 3019) in relation to the 1973 Constitution; she could not be charged with plunder because the Anti-Plunder Law was enacted only after Marcos was ousted. Forfeiture was not part of the criminal judgment because separate civil suits exist to recover the Swiss-foundation millions, though the judgment perpetually disqualified her from public office. She was granted bail because none of her offenses was a capital one; her original P150,000 bond was forfeited due to her absence at promulgation, an arrest order was issued November 9, 2018, and she posted a new P150,000 bond on November 16, with PJ Rafael R. Lagos ordering her release the same day. Panganiban flags as strange that only Lagos signed the release order (without his Fifth Division co-members Mendoza-Arcega and Mañalac), that her 'Motion for Leave of Court to Avail of Post-Conviction Remedies' had not yet been ruled upon, and that the prosecution did not object to and meekly accepted the bail grant.
